Making a continuous flight auger (CFA) pile, from positioning the rig to the finished pile
Deep foundations › Piles › Replacement (bored) pile › Partial displacement › Continuous flight auger (CFA)
Fresh concrete under pressure, with the concrete head above the toe
The rotary head turns the hollow-stem auger and pushes it down to the design depth. The spoil is not removed: the soil held on the flights supports the bore wall all the way.
No casing or bentonite slurry is needed, and groundwater is no problem. The bottom of the stem is closed by a flap (in practice a sacrificial plug), so no soil or water gets into the hollow stem.
At the design depth the auger is lifted 15–30 cm and the pump forces concrete down the hollow stem: the pressure opens the flap (blows out the plug) and the concrete emerges below the auger.
The auger is withdrawn under concrete pressure, without rotation or turning very slowly: the concrete fills the bore below the toe, the auger brings up the soil and the auger cleaner strips it off.

The on-board computer records the concrete pressure at the top of the auger and the concrete volume for every metre (theoretical + 15–20 %). The pile is concreted up to working level, without vibration.
The pile has been concreted up to working level. The excavator clears the spoil around the fresh pile head, and the rig moves straight on to the next pile: one rig makes 15–30 piles a day.
Straight after concreting the crane lowers the reinforcement cage into the still fresh, fluid concrete. The spacers ensure the concrete cover.
Down to 6–10 m the cage sinks under its own weight; deeper it is helped by a vibrator. The longitudinal bars project above the concrete for the later connection.
Time jump: the concrete has hardened. The pile head is cut down to the design level, the starter bars are left exposed, and then the pile cap is built.
The finished CFA pile: a solid concrete shaft socketed into the bearing stratum, reinforced at the top. A fast, quiet, low-vibration technique, with no casing or slurry.
